title: Everything we knew about software has changed — Theo Browne, @t3dotgg ​
talk_summary: Theo Browne argues that model capability jumps (tool-calling, long-horizon tasks, self-orchestration) mean developers should attempt much larger scopes and discard inherited habits like terminal-centric workflows and fear of deleting code. His concrete example is replacing a PR-triage service with a single markdown prompt run on a cron that reviews PRs and publishes a prioritized HTML report.

takeaways.what_they_do: A prompt file enumerates repos, inspects open PRs, assesses status, prioritizes work, then writes a static HTML report to S3 and returns a URL, triggered by cron each morning.
takeaways.evidence_quote: go to these four GitHub repos, look at all the open PRs, figure out what the current status of the work is, and then help me prioritize it

takeaways.technique: Prompt-level self-orchestration instead of custom scaffolding
takeaways.what_they_do: Claims newer models can spawn sub-models, decompose work, and verify results when simply prompted, reducing need for custom orchestration software.
takeaways.evidence_quote: You don't need some custom tooling, some custom system, some fancy software factory. You just need to prompt it to go a little further.

takeaways.what_they_do: Argues against guilt-merging mediocre PRs and for deleting code/resetting when the approach is wrong, since agent work is cheap to redo.
takeaways.evidence_quote: why are we so scared of deleting code? ... we have such a bad sunk cost mindset in this industry

takeaways.what_they_do: Frames current dev practice (terminals, env-file secrecy, language identity) as skeuomorphic habits worth questioning when agent capability changes.
takeaways.evidence_quote: is this how we do things cuz it's right, or is this how we do things cuz it's just how we've always done it?
